parts.headline: The Bubble Is in the Denominator
parts.question: Does the hardware hold its value?

call.line: The market is not cheap. It is capitalizing AI earnings before anyone knows who owns them.
actions: Hold the 5.26% earnings yield (19.0 times earnings) against the 10-year: when the bond pays more, stocks offer no risk premium.
Stress-test the 29.5% earnings growth for server lives and depreciation before you pay for it.
Treat the $250 billion of hyperscaler bonds as competition for the savings that set the discount rate.
flips: Used-chip values and server lives hold after scarcity fades.
Productivity turns higher and lab revenue compounds toward the checks the infrastructure requires.

notes.label: What the denominator is made of
notes.text: Earnings, not multiples (Ren): tech's forward multiple up about 14% since October 2022, against 250% in the run to March 2000. Made by the buildout (George, Silverio): tech is 76% of S&P profit growth, half of it from AI spending. Paid for with bonds (Kunimoto): close to $250B of hyperscaler high-grade bonds in 2026.

tests.event: Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon report; depreciation, server lives and 29.5% growth will test the earnings denominator.

source.ref: Company earnings calendar, date via Financial Modeling Prep

resolver.rule: Sum depreciation and amortization, and sum operating income, for the four companies for the September quarter of 2026 and of 2025, from each release or 10-Q; a year-over-year growth rate for depreciation above the rate for operating income resolves confirmed, equal or below resolves refuted. A change to server useful lives disclosed in the same filings is the owner's reading into the Result, not the verdict.

relations.mechanism: The S&P 500 trades at 19.0 times forward earnings, and the market looks cheaper because profits surged. Those profits depend on AI spending: capital spending becomes supplier revenue and reported profit, so the denominator of the multiple is partly the buildout itself, while about $250 billion of hyperscaler bonds issued through August compete for the savings that set the discount rate, with the 10-year Treasury at 5.31 percent on October 5. Whether the profits are real depends on whether the hardware holds its value: if used-chip prices fall once scarcity fades and server lives prove shorter than the schedules, depreciation grows faster than operating income and the earnings being capitalized belong to no one yet. The Call would change if chip values held, productivity turned higher and lab revenue compounded.
alternatives: The hardware earns because it is used: GPUs are already running hot while the data says adoption and utilization are still early, so the capacity is not idle collateral (the case David George makes).

Old chips still rent at a price: contracted lease rates and second-hand prices have held for chips launched three to six years ago, and compute is about 60 percent of hyperscaler capex (the case JunkBondInvestor makes).

The checks are arriving: OpenAI's recurring revenue is nearing $70 billion, with enterprise sales more than doubled since July, so the earnings being capitalized have an owner (the case Tae Kim makes).
The rise is earnings, not multiples: tech's forward multiple is up about 14 percent since October 2022, against 250 percent in the run to March 2000, so this is not 1999 (the case Ren makes).
